## Robustness Assessment
<!-- [PLACEHOLDER] -->

This section shifts from training stochasticity to
sensitivity to modeling choices. The question is whether the
conclusions for the current high-frequency TD3 setup would
change materially under nearby alternatives in feature specification, reward
definition, transaction-cost assumptions, or split design.

The goal is to separate results that appear structural from results that may
depend too heavily on one narrow experimental setup.

```{python}
#| label: robustness_setup
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

import pandas as pd

from thesis_mlflow_results import audit_plots_enabled, load_experiment_snapshot, runs_overview_table, show_table_meta

EXPERIMENT_NAME = "pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected_dsr"
snapshot = load_experiment_snapshot(EXPERIMENT_NAME)
finished = snapshot.latest_finished
runs_df = runs_overview_table(EXPERIMENT_NAME)
_audit = audit_plots_enabled()
```


## H2: Feature Specification Sensitivity
<!-- [PLACEHOLDER] -->

This section compares three feature-specification levels under otherwise
identical conditions (same algorithm, data, reward, and transaction cost) to
assess whether richer microstructure-aware state representations improve
out-of-sample performance.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
```{=latex}
\begin{landscape}
```
:::

```{python}
#| label: h2_feature_comparison
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| tbl-cap: "H2 feature sensitivity: test-split metrics for minimal (3), selected (10), and full (33) feature sets."

from thesis_mlflow_results import load_scenario_metrics
from thesis_tables import build_comparison_rows, comparison_table_html

_H2_SCENARIOS = [
    ("pooled_td3_h3_features_minimal",                           "Minimal (3 features)",   False),
    ("pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected", "Selected (10 features)", True),
    ("pooled_td3_h3_features_full",                              "Full (33 features)",     False),
]

_H2_COLS = [
    ("sharpe_ratio",          "Sharpe",   ".3f"),
    ("sortino_ratio",         "Sortino",  ".3f"),
    ("total_return",          "Return",   ".2e"),
    ("max_drawdown",          "Max DD",   ".2e"),
    ("win_rate",              "Win Rate", ".2%"),
    ("profit_factor",         "PF",       ".3f"),
    ("turnover",              "Turnover", ".4f"),
    ("annualized_volatility", "Ann. Vol", ".3f"),
]

_HIGHER_BETTER = {
    "sharpe_ratio": True, "sortino_ratio": True, "total_return": True,
    "max_drawdown": False, "win_rate": True, "profit_factor": True, "annualized_volatility": False,
}

scenario_metrics = [(label, load_scenario_metrics(exp), is_base) for exp, label, is_base in _H2_SCENARIOS]
rows = build_comparison_rows(scenario_metrics, _H2_COLS, index_col="Feature Set", higher_better=_HIGHER_BETTER)

if all(row.get("Sharpe", "—") == "—" for row in rows):
    print("No H2 results available. Run: uv run thesis-experiments h2")
else:
    display(comparison_table_html(rows, _H2_COLS, index_col="Feature Set"))
    show_table_meta(finished, audit=_audit)
```

::: {.table-note}
**Source:** Author's own calculations.
**Legend:** Sharpe: mean excess return / std (not annualized). Sortino: mean excess return / downside deviation (not annualized). Return: cumulative simple return. Max DD: maximum drawdown. Win Rate: fraction of positive-return steps. PF: profit factor (gross wins / gross losses). Turnover: mean absolute position change per step. Ann. Vol: annualized volatility.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
```{=latex}
\end{landscape}
```
:::

The feature comparison supports a qualified version of H2. The minimal
three-feature representation produces a negative cumulative return
($-3.45 \times 10^{-8}$), a profit factor below one, and a short-biased policy
that spends 77.2% of the evaluation window short. The selected 10-feature
microstructure representation improves the result to a positive cumulative
return ($1.29 \times 10^{-7}$), a profit factor of 2.01, and a materially
stronger Sortino ratio under the same data and evaluation protocol.

The full 33-feature representation does not improve further. It remains
positive on cumulative return ($2.68 \times 10^{-8}$), but underperforms the
selected representation on return, drawdown, profit factor, and turnover. This
suggests that the benefit comes from adding relevant microstructure information,
not from maximizing feature count. For this thesis, H2 is therefore supported
for the transition from a minimal snapshot representation to the selected
microstructure-aware state, but not for the claim that every broader feature set
is better.

## H3: Sensitivity Analysis
<!-- [PLACEHOLDER] -->

This section reports reward-design and transaction-cost sensitivity. Feature
specification is reported separately in H2 above. Each axis holds all other
design choices constant. The shared baseline across both H3 axes is the selected
10-feature set with log return reward and zero transaction cost.

```{python}
#| label: h3_sensitivity_tables
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown, display
from thesis_mlflow_results import load_scenario_metrics
from thesis_tables import fmt_val, display_df, table_note

_H3_AXES = [
    {
        "label": "Reward Function Design",
        "col": "Variant",
        "scenarios": [
            ("pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected",     "Log Return (baseline)", True),
            ("pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected_dsr", "Differential Sharpe (DSR)", False),
        ],
    },
    {
        "label": "Transaction Costs",
        "col": "Fees",
        "scenarios": [
            ("pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected", "0 bp (baseline)", True),
            ("pooled_td3_h3_fees_1e6",                                   "0.01 bp",         False),
            ("pooled_td3_h3_fees_1e5",                                   "0.1 bp",          False),
            ("pooled_td3_h3_fees_1e4",                                   "1 bp",            False),
        ],
    },
]

_H3_COLS = [
    ("sharpe_ratio",  "Sharpe",   ".3f"),
    ("sortino_ratio", "Sortino",  ".3f"),
    ("total_return",  "Return",   ".2e"),
    ("max_drawdown",  "Max DD",   ".2e"),
    ("win_rate",      "Win Rate", ".2%"),
    ("profit_factor", "PF",       ".3f"),
    ("turnover",      "Turnover", ".4f"),
]

for axis in _H3_AXES:
    rows = []
    for exp, label, _ in axis["scenarios"]:
        m = load_scenario_metrics(exp)
        row = {axis["col"]: label}
        for key, col, fmt in _H3_COLS:
            row[col] = fmt_val(m.get(key), fmt)
        rows.append(row)
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    if df.iloc[:, 1:].isin(["—"]).all().all():
        print(f"{axis['label']}: no results yet. Run: uv run thesis-experiments h3")
    else:
        display(Markdown(f"### {axis['label']}"))
        display_df(df)
        table_note(source="Author's own calculations.")
        show_table_meta(finished, audit=_audit)
```

The reward-design comparison shows that Differential Sharpe Ratio optimization
changes the learned policy in an economically meaningful direction. Relative to
the log-return baseline, the DSR run increases cumulative return from
$1.29 \times 10^{-7}$ to $2.28 \times 10^{-7}$, improves profit factor from
2.01 to 5.70, and reduces maximum drawdown from $-1.93 \times 10^{-7}$ to
$-1.05 \times 10^{-7}$. The DSR policy is also more balanced in exposure,
moving from an 86.7% long policy under log-return reward to an approximately
neutral 49.8% long and 50.2% short distribution. This supports the reward-design
part of H3: the reward objective materially affects both performance and policy
behavior.

The transaction-cost comparison places a sharper bound on the economic claim.
At 0.01 basis points the TD3 policy remains marginally positive
($2.28 \times 10^{-7}$) but with a weaker profit factor than the zero-fee DSR
run. At 0.1 basis points, cumulative return turns negative
($-7.60 \times 10^{-7}$), and at 1 basis point the loss increases to
$-5.89 \times 10^{-6}$. The direction of the result is unambiguous: the
observed edge exists only under very low transaction-cost assumptions. This
supports H3 and also limits the practical interpretation of H1.

Overall, the robustness evidence is strongest for feature specification,
reward-design sensitivity, and transaction-cost sensitivity. It is not yet
strong evidence of robustness across market regimes, longer samples, alternative
chronological splits, or repeated random seeds.

## H4: Learning Progression Check

This section addresses a more fundamental robustness question: whether the
algorithm is actually learning at all, rather than converging to a policy that
merely appears competent due to favorable initialization or dataset quirks. The
approach is to run multiple short trials (200k steps each) and test whether the
agent reliably outperforms a dummy strategy.

### Experimental Design

The H4 experiment runs $N$ independent trials of the baseline TD3 configuration
(selected 10 features, DSR reward, zero fees) with limited training steps.
Each trial is initialized with a different random seed and evaluated on the same
held-out test split. The key question is whether the distribution of trial
outcomes shows systematic learning rather than random variation around zero.

```{python}
#| label: h4_learning_progression
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| tbl-cap: "H4 learning progression: performance statistics across multiple short trials."

import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Image, display
from thesis_mlflow_results import load_h4_report
from thesis_tables import display_df, table_note

_H4_SCENARIO = "pooled_td3_hft_lob_state_space_pooled_streaming_selected_dsr_h4_n5"

h4_data = load_h4_report(_H4_SCENARIO)

if h4_data:
    stats = h4_data.get("statistics", {})
    criteria = h4_data.get("criteria", {})
    trials = h4_data.get("trials", [])

    # Summary statistics table
    summary_rows = [
        ("N Trials", stats.get("n_trials", len(trials))),
        ("Mean Return", f"{stats.get('mean_return', 0):.2e}"),
        ("Std Return", f"{stats.get('std_return', 0):.2e}"),
        ("Mean Sharpe Ratio", f"{stats.get('mean_sharpe', 0):.3f}"),
        ("Mean Win Rate", f"{stats.get('mean_win_rate', 0):.1%}"),
    ]

    if "p_value_return" in stats:
        p_val = stats.get("p_value_return", 1)
        p_str = f"{p_val:.4f}"
        p_sig = "*" if p_val < 0.05 else ""
        summary_rows.append(("Return p-value (vs zero)", f"{p_str}{p_sig}"))

    summary_df = pd.DataFrame(summary_rows, columns=["Metric", "Value"])
    display(summary_df)

    # Criteria table
    criteria_rows = [
        ("Positive mean return", criteria.get("positive_return", False)),
        ("Positive mean Sharpe", criteria.get("positive_sharpe", False)),
        ("Significant return (p<0.05)", criteria.get("significant_return", False)),
        ("Win rate > 50%", criteria.get("win_rate_above_baseline", False)),
    ]

    criteria_display = [
        (label, "[green]PASS[/green]" if passed else "[red]FAIL[/red]")
        for label, passed in criteria_rows
    ]
    criteria_df = pd.DataFrame(criteria_display, columns=["Criterion", "Status"])

    criteria_met = criteria.get("criteria_met", "0/0")
    overall = criteria.get("overall", False)
    verdict = "[green]PASS[/green]" if overall else "[yellow]FAIL[/yellow]"

    print(f"\n**Learning Criteria Check:** {criteria_met} met")
    display_df(criteria_df)
    print(f"**Overall Verdict:** {verdict}")

    # Individual trials table
    if trials:
        trial_df = pd.DataFrame(trials)
        display_cols = ["trial", "total_return", "sharpe_ratio", "win_rate", "profit_factor", "vs_dummy_return"]
        if all(c in trial_df.columns for c in display_cols):
            view = trial_df[display_cols].copy()
            view["vs_dummy_return"] = view["vs_dummy_return"].apply(
                lambda x: f"{x:.2e}" if isinstance(x, (int, float)) else x
            )
            view["win_rate"] = view["win_rate"].apply(lambda x: f"{x:.1%}")
            view.columns = ["Trial", "Return", "Sharpe", "Win Rate", "Profit Factor", "vs Dummy"]
            display_df(view)
    table_note(source="Author's own calculations.")
    show_table_meta(finished, audit=_audit)
else:
    print("No H4 results available. Run: uv run thesis-experiments h4")
```

### Interpretation of H4 Results

The H4 design complements the single-run evidence reported in H1-H3 by
directly testing learning capability. A positive result here would mean that the
algorithm, when given a relatively short training budget (200k steps versus
several million in the main experiments), consistently produces policies that
outperform a random baseline. This addresses the concern that the reported
H1-H3 edge might reflect favorable initialization rather than genuine learning.

A negative result — where the agent fails to demonstrate statistically
significant improvement across trials — would not invalidate H1-H3, but it would
temper the interpretation. It would suggest that the observed performance
requires either longer training, more favorable initialization conditions, or
that the learned edge is smaller than the single-run results imply.

For the current experimental package, H4 provides the seed-level robustness
check identified as a gap in the robustness matrix above. When combined with the
H2 and H3 sensitivities, it offers a more complete picture of whether the
TD3 agent's performance is structural or artifact-dependent.
